action: Federal contractors: confirm you hold a current System Security Plan and a working plan of action and milestones for NIST SP 800-171 contracts, and that access to government information is actually controlled.
exec: Missing security paperwork alone, with no reported breach, cost a federal contractor $5 million; whistleblowers drove the case.
plain: Building-systems company Johnson Controls will pay $5 million to settle US government claims that it did not follow the cybersecurity rules written into its federal contracts.

key_findings: Johnson Controls, Inc., Johnson Controls Fire Protection LP and Johnson Controls Security Solutions LLC agreed to pay $5 million; liability was not determined.
The government alleged they failed to control access to protected government information because they lacked knowledge of and control over their own systems.
On contracts requiring NIST SP 800-171, including Defense work, they allegedly lacked a compliant System Security Plan and a fully implemented plan of action and milestones.
The conduct covers January 2018 to August 2025 on contracts with NASA and the Departments of Defense, Energy and Justice.
The settlement resolves two whistleblower suits; a former employee receives $850,000. No data breach is reported.
recommendations: The release gives no compliance steps; it states that contract cybersecurity requirements are binding and that agencies will pursue contractors who fail to meet them.
Contractors under NIST SP 800-171 should hold the System Security Plan and plan of action and milestones the release says were missing.

summary: The Justice Department said Johnson Controls, Inc. and two subsidiaries agreed to pay $5 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations that they did not meet cybersecurity requirements in contracts and subcontracts with NASA and the Departments of Defense, Energy and Justice from January 2018 to August 2025. The claims are allegations only and the release reports no breach. One whistleblower receives $850,000.
title: DOJ: Johnson Controls and two subsidiaries pay $5 million over federal contract cybersecurity failings

validation.note: Reviewed against the original US Department of Justice document.
